  1320  Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers.
  1321      \113\ See Annual Report 2020 and GAO 19-297, supra notes 76 and 
  1322  81.
  1323  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1324  
  1325      Accordingly, DHS notes that without the fees proposed in this 
  1326  rulemaking, it cannot administer OPT consistent with its focus on 
  1327  protecting American workers and may shut down the program entirely.
  1328  
  1329  C. Establishing the Optional Practical Training Fees
  1330  
  1331      After considering the problematic issues plaguing the practical 
  1332  training programs in recent years and substantial rise in participants, 
  1333  as discussed above in section IV.A-C, DHS believes that program fees 
  1334  are necessary for all types of OPT. DHS believes that its mission in 
  1335  combating fraud, as well as protecting U.S. workers and upholding the 
  1336  integrity of the immigration system, would be furthered through a fee, 
  1337  which would deter the participation by adverse actors and increase the 
  1338  level of oversight and scrutiny by schools when endorsing OPT for its 
  1339  students.
  1340      As noted above, DHS believes that absent these fees, it will not be 
  1341  able to operate OPT consistent with its focus on preventing fraud and 
  1342  protecting American workers and may shut down the program entirely.
  1343      Specifically, DHS believes this proposed fee would incentivize 
  1344  educational institutions to exercise greater oversight and selectivity 
  1345  when recommending students for OPT, thereby reducing fraudulent 
  1346  authorizations and curbing ``visa mill'' activities. By establishing a 
  1347  financial obligation through a fee, this proposed rule would encourage 
  1348  schools to ensure that OPT opportunities provide genuine educational 
  1349  value that aligns with the original intent of the practical training 
  1350  program, thereby promoting shared responsibility and accountability. 
  1351  Schools would have a direct stake in the integrity of the OPT program, 
  1352  incentivizing them to strengthen their internal compliance and 
  1353  selection processes and only issue OPT recommendations to those 
  1354  students for whom the school will pay the required fee. The financial 
  1355  costs would deter schools from recommending students with questionable 
  1356  qualifications for OPT, leading to higher program integrity. DHS 
  1357  anticipates that schools will consider adopting internal policies and 
  1358  procedures that prioritize quality and compliance over quantity of 
  1359  participants, stabilizing the number of OPT participants. This fee 
  1360  would result in a smaller pool of participants, as schools would be 
  1361  more selective in determining which students are qualified to 
  1362  participate in OPT. In turn, the rule, as proposed, would effectively 
  1363  eliminate students who engage in OPT as a pathway for low-paid 
  1364  employment or those who are trying to circumvent the H-1B visa cap and 
  1365  fee requirements, as they would no longer be able to obtain 
  1366  ``automatic'' recommendations for OPT from their schools. DHS believes 
  1367  that this proposed fee would incentivize schools to only recommend the 
  1368  most promising students to engage in OPT after a thorough review and 
  1369  payment of the required fee. Limiting the pool of OPT participants to 
  1370  talented students who are in genuine educational programs and placed in 
  1371  training programs that directly relate to their major area of study 
  1372  would protect the interests and jobs of American workers in the long 
  1373  run. The proposed rule would alleviate the job market from depressed 
  1374  wages and low-paid jobs otherwise held by F-1 nonimmigrant students. 
  1375  Additionally, the proposed rule would curb the number of students and 
  1376  employers attempting to circumvent the H-1B visa cap and fee, and thus, 
  1377  result in less replacement of U.S. workers, as schools would have 
  1378  greater equity and stake than employers in determining who participates 
  1379  in OPT due to their financial responsibilities.
  1380      A reduction in the pool of OPT applicants, along with the 
  1381  stabilization of participant numbers, would alleviate DHS's resource 
  1382  burden tied to enforcement activities related to OPT and enable the 
  1383  agency to conduct more focused and efficient oversight of SEVP 
  1384  programs. Enhanced school compliance would reduce the investigative and 
  1385  enforcement burden on DHS, allowing limited resources to be focused on 
  1386  higher-priority cases. Specifically, it would allow SEVP to 
  1387  strategically allocate resources to other programs that it administers 
  1388  and regulates. With fewer applicants to monitor, SEVP would be able to 
  1389  focus its investigative efforts on high-risk industries and sectors 
  1390  where OPT abuse is more likely to occur, such as technology and 
  1391  critical infrastructure. This targeted approach would enable
  1392  
  1393  [[Page 64575]]
  1394  
  1395  more thorough reviews of participating students and schools, while 
  1396  freeing up personnel to support other programs managed by SEVP, 
  1397  including OPT and CPT, and provide heightened customer service and 
  1398  technical support to educational institutions and other stakeholders. 
  1399  In turn, by streamlining operational planning and focusing resources 
  1400  where vulnerabilities are greatest, DHS would improve the quality and 
  1401  effectiveness of compliance checks, fraud detection, and enforcement 
  1402  actions, ultimately strengthening the integrity of the OPT program and 
  1403  related SEVP initiatives.
  1404      This streamlining and strategic allocation of DHS resources, 
  1405  combined with the reporting requirements under 20 U.S.C. 1011f of the 
  1406  Higher Education Act that are already in place will enable law 
  1407  enforcement to detect, analyze, and investigate suspicious financial 
  1408  transactions tied to foreign governments or threat actors that may seek 
  1409  to use OPT to steal US technology or advance other national security 
  1410  threats. Generally, schools would need to track how they are funding 
  1411  the OPT fees in their financial reports and disclosures for accounting 
  1412  purposes. These reporting and accounting mechanisms could aid law 
  1413  enforcement in tracking the origin and purpose of the funds. Since the 
  1414  funding of OPT participation is costly and requires transparency, the 
  1415  OPT fee could expose attempts by foreign adversaries to subsidize these 
  1416  costs through targeted investments or donations to schools offering OPT 
  1417  to F-1 nonimmigrant students. For example, large or unusual financial 
  1418  contributions from foreign sources, especially those tied to programs 
  1419  that rely heavily on OPT, could serve as red flags for further 
  1420  investigation into fraud and national security concerns.
  1421      Furthermore, INA 274A(h)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324a(h)(1), notes that, 
  1422  ``[i]n providing documentation or endorsement of authorization of 
  1423  aliens . . . authorized to be employed in the United States, the 
  1424  Attorney General shall provide that any limitations with respect to the 
  1425  period or type of employment or employer shall be conspicuously stated 
  1426  on the documentation or endorsement.'' As such, DHS believes the 
  1427  financial obligation of the proposed fee, in tandem with the 
  1428  requirement that SEVP-certified institutions provide proof of payment 
  1429  of this fee when submitting a recommendation for OPT, also serves as a 
  1430  deterrent to schools, foreign students, and employers seeking to abuse 
  1431  OPT.
  1432      DHS believes that this proposed rule does not need to define which 
  1433  OPT experiences provide genuine educational value that is directly 
  1434  related to the F-1 nonimmigrant student's major area of study, given 
  1435  that the current regulations provide the eligibility framework for OPT 
  1436  and schools are in a better position to assess the weight and value of 
  1437  hands-on educational programs offered through OPT. Moreover, this 
  1438  proposed fee rule does not propose the imposition of specific 
  1439  limitations or restrictions on how the schools should collect or source 
  1440  the requisite funds to make the fee payments for each student engaged 
  1441  in OPT, to the extent that the school complies with all other 
  1442  applicable laws, including reporting foreign gifts and contracts under 
  1443  20 U.S.C. 1011f. DHS acknowledges that the schools may pass the 
  1444  financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant 
  1445  students, all students, or employers. If the proposed fee is passed on 
  1446  to F-1 nonimmigrant students or employers, it would further discourage 
  1447  misuse of OPT by increasing the cost of participation for those whose 
  1448  intent is primarily to work or reside in the U.S. without legitimate 
  1449  academic purpose and for employers displacing U.S. workers.
  1450      While DHS understands that the proposed fees are not nominal 
  1451  amounts, such costs are reasonably related to the purposes of INA 
  1452  101(a)(15)(F)(i), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(F)(i),\114\ and this proposed 
  1453  rule which addresses the vulnerabilities of OPT. Furthermore, these 
  1454  fees are intended to discourage aliens from using the OPT program to 
  1455  market themselves to employers seeking to bypass H-1B caps, fees, and 
  1456  prevailing wage requirements. In weighing the educational costs and the 
  1457  value of hands-on training experience in the United States, DHS 
  1458  believes that the OPT fees are on par with the educational costs that 
  1459  foreign students incur for one or two years of education in a program 
  1460  of study in the United States. However, DHS acknowledges that there may 
  1461  be instances in which a refund of the payment is necessary when OPT 
  1462  does not proceed as initially intended. The proposed rule includes 
  1463  refund provisions so that educational institutions may seek a refund if 
  1464  the student does not receive an OPT employment authorization document.
  1465  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1466  
  1467      \114\ See Narenji, 617 F.2d at 745.
  1468  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1469  
  1470      The proposed rule intends for schools to pay the applicable fees 
  1471  for eligible students who will engage in a form of OPT, regardless of 
  1472  the manner in which the foreign student obtained F-1 status--whether 
  1473  admitted in F-1 status or through a change of status (COS) within the 
  1474  United States--and irrespective of how the F-1 student obtained an 
  1475  extension of stay when seeking to engage in a form of OPT. In other 
  1476  words, the proposed fee would apply equally for all schools and 
  1477  students seeking to engage in OPT, regardless of whether the F-1 
  1478  student received an Extension of Stay (EOS) authorization through USCIS 
  1479  or through CBP after traveling abroad to obtain a new I-94 to engage in 
  1480  OPT.
  1481      DHS proposes to establish two different OPT fee amounts. DHS 
  1482  believes that the initial OPT fee amount should be higher than the 
  1483  subsequent fee amounts because, when nonimmigrant students initially 
  1484  apply for employment authorization, they may not have been vetted by 
  1485  the U.S. Government since their initial application for an F-1 visa and 
  1486  subsequent admission into the country.\115\ The importance of ensuring 
  1487  integrity in the OPT program is most prevalent at this stage. For the 
  1488  initial fee, DHS also considered the possibility that nonimmigrants 
  1489  could undermine the H-1B visa payment by abusing OPT.\116\ As such, DHS 
  1490  selected a fee amount for OPT comparable to the fee for H-1B visas 
  1491  \117\ that would deter visa fraud. The fee amount is designed to 
  1492  closely align with the H-1B fees to reduce students and employers from 
  1493  using OPT to circumvent the H-1B visa program fees. Schools would have 
  1494  to pay the OPT fee prior to the DSO entering the recommendation for OPT 
  1495  in SEVIS. To be clear, no DSO would be able to enter an OPT 
  1496  recommendation without the school having paid the applicable fee. 
  1497  Through this rule, DHS intends to verify whether the schools have made 
  1498  OPT fee payments for each student that they recommend for OPT,
  1499  
  1500  [[Page 64576]]
  1501  
  1502  thereby strengthening the integrity of the program.
  1503  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1504  
  1505      \115\ DHS recognizes that the application requirements for EOS 
  1506  under 8 CFR 214.1(c) and 214.2(f)(7)(v) may provide DHS with 
  1507  additional opportunities to vet F-1 nonimmigrant students. See 
  1508  ``Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of 
  1509  Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange 
  1510  Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media,'' 91 FR 
  1511  44976 (July 17, 2026). This final rule (hereinafter ``Duration of 
  1512  Status Final Rule'') amended the admission period for F nonimmigrant 
  1513  classification from duration of status to a fixed time period and 
  1514  implemented additional changes to admission and extension 
  1515  requirements. However, not all F-1 nonimmigrant students are 
  1516  required to apply for an EOS to engage OPT, such as those 
  1517  participating in pre-completion OPT or those grandfathered under the 
  1518  Duration of Status Final Rule and subject to the regulations at 8 
  1519  CFR 214.2(m). DHS believes that the regulations currently in effect, 
  1520  together with the proposed OPT fee rule, will provide a 
  1521  comprehensive and holistic approach for DHS to effectively regulate 
  1522  the OPT program.
  1523      \116\ See Proclamation No. 10973, 90 FR (Sept. 19, 2025), 
  1524  Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers.
  1525      \117\ Id.
  1526  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1527  
  1528      Notably, the proposed OPT fees collected under this rule would be 
  1529  deposited in the Treasury of the United States as a miscellaneous 
  1530  receipt pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 3302. ICE would not maintain or use the 
  1531  funding collected under these OPT fee provisions promulgated pursuant 
  1532  to INA 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184, because the statute does not provide 
  1533  legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected. While the OPT 
  1534  fees would be deposited into the Treasury of the United States and not 
  1535  specifically earmarked for ICE SEVP or immigration enforcement 
  1536  activities, the collection of these fees remain essential in addressing 
  1537  the vulnerabilities of the OPT program for the reasons explained in 
  1538  this section. It is also conceivable that funds collected could later 
  1539  be effectively appropriated by Congress to various government agencies 
  1540  to further enhance the integrity of the immigration system. However, 
  1541  the deterrent nature of the OPT fee remains regardless of whether these 
  1542  funds are appropriated by Congress to government agencies for this 
  1543  purpose.
  1544      DHS considered some alternative regulatory approaches to address 
  1545  the issues in OPT that were discussed in sections IV.A. and IV.B. of 
  1546  the rule, such as applying STEM OPT requirements like site visits, 
  1547  training plans, and additional reporting to OPT more generally. 
  1548  However, DHS ultimately determined that proposing a fee for 
  1549  participation in the OPT program would offer an immediate and effective 
  1550  means to strengthen the integrity of OPT with minimal administrative 
  1551  burdens on the government. Unlike more complex regulatory alternatives, 
  1552  such as expanded site visits, increased reporting requirements, 
  1553  additional processes, and stricter procedural mandates, a fee can be 
  1554  implemented quickly and uniformly across all participants. This 
  1555  approach does not require DHS to deploy significant additional 
  1556  resources for enforcement or oversight. Moreover, the effect of a 
  1557  financial commitment is nearly immediate--those seeking to abuse the 
  1558  program are less likely to invest in participation when faced with a 
  1559  tangible cost, making engagement in OPT for nefarious purposes less 
  1560  attractive to bad actors. Furthermore, the financial commitment of this 
  1561  fee may encourage schools to apply a heightened level of scrutiny when 
  1562  reviewing an F-1 nonimmigrant student's request for OPT to ensure that 
  1563  the student is engaging in a legitimate OPT opportunity.
  1564      Although STEM OPT has regulatory safeguards, including reporting 
  1565  obligations, employer site visits, and the Form I-983 training plan 
  1566  requirement, DHS does not believe that simply extending those 
  1567  requirements to the initial period of post-completion OPT would be 
  1568  sufficient as an initial response to the overarching OPT program 
  1569  integrity concerns. Experience with STEM OPT indicates that additional 
  1570  procedural and documentation requirements, while useful, do not 
  1571  eliminate the risk of fraud, abuse, or noncompliance and may require 
  1572  substantial time and resources to implement, monitor, and enforce 
  1573  effectively. Solutions requiring self-attestations, reporting, or 
  1574  reliance on an honor system, without more, are insufficient to ensure 
  1575  the integrity of the OPT program. These mechanisms would need to be 
  1576  paired with enforcement activity, such as conducting more site visits 
  1577  across a broader range of employers, which may function less as a 
  1578  proactive fraud-prevention measure and more as reactive response to 
  1579  violations after they occur. In contrast, by requiring a financial 
  1580  commitment through an OPT fee, DHS would encourage participant to 
  1581  demonstrate a seriousness and genuine intent to comply with program 
  1582  requirements. The fee establishes a tangible stake in the process, 
  1583  helping to distinguish those who are committed to lawful participation 
  1584  from those who may seek to exploit the program. In addition to the 
  1585  current regulatory mechanisms in place, this additional layer of 
  1586  accountability supports the Department's broader efforts to uphold the 
  1587  integrity and effectiveness of the OPT program.
  1588      The Department recognizes the importance of restoring and 
  1589  maintaining public confidence in the OPT program through an immediate, 
  1590  effective regulatory solution, rather than a complex bureaucratic 
  1591  framework that may take years to yield results. By proposing a fee, 
  1592  rather than alternative administrative procedures, the Department seeks 
  1593  to minimize overregulation and complexities while responding to serious 
  1594  program integrity concerns that cannot be addressed quickly through 
  1595  such procedures alone. Recent concerns regarding misuse and fraud and 
  1596  the displacement of American workers have underscored the need for 
  1597  visible, effective action to reinforce the integrity of the program. 
  1598  The fee serves as a clear signal to the public and stakeholders that 
  1599  the Department is taking meaningful steps to safeguard the OPT program, 
  1600  while ensuring that legitimate participants continue to benefit from 
  1601  its opportunities.
  1602      DHS believes the OPT fee is a crucial first step to urgently 
  1603  address fraud, abuse, and noncompliance, in a targeted and immediately 
  1604  implementable manner. This measured approach allows for ongoing 
  1605  evaluation of the fee's impact and effectiveness, providing the agency 
  1606  with valuable data to inform future policy decisions. Importantly, the 
  1607  implementation of a fee should not be interpreted as precluding future 
  1608  changes to the OPT program through additional regulatory requirements; 
  1609  rather, it represents an immediate first step in a graduated strategy 
  1610  to address the urgent program integrity concerns. The Department seeks 
  1611  to retain flexibility to pursue additional regulatory measures in the 
  1612  future should further action be warranted.
  1613      In considering fees, DHS carefully evaluated various fee options, 
  1614  including exemptions to the fee for small educational institutions. See 
  1615  sec. VII.B.6. However, DHS estimates that 56 percent of regulated SEVP-
  1616  certified institutions are small entities. Id. This approach could 
  1617  leave significant fraud vulnerabilities unaddressed, given that many 
  1618  SEVP-certified institutions are small entities. Various factors and 
  1619  data were considered in this proposed rule, as explained in section 
  1620  VII.B.6.
  1621      Separately, DHS acknowledges that OPT is not the only practical 
  1622  training program with the potential for significant fraud and national 
  1623  security issues. Fraud and national security threats in CPT have also 
  1624  been historically prevalent and have increased along with the number of 
  1625  students engaging in CPT. DHS will continue to monitor these concerning 
  1626  trends within the CPT program and will take additional actions as 
  1627  necessary.
  1628  
  1629  D. Technical Edits
  1630  
  1631      The addition of an OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13 would require 
  1632  clarifying that the other fees listed under the current regulations are 
  1633  solely in reference to SEVP fees, as evidenced by the section heading 
  1634  titled ``SEVIS fee for certain F, J, and M nonimmigrants.'' \118\ The 
  1635  proposed rule would add provisions regarding OPT fees under this 
  1636  section, such that it would be necessary to clarify which fees are 
  1637  specific SEVP fees and which are OPT fees.
  1638  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1639  
  1640      \118\ See 8 CFR 214.13 (current) (emphasis added).
  1641  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1642  
  1643  V. Discussion of Changes
  1644  
  1645  A. Establishing a Fee for Initial and Any Subsequent OPT
  1646  
  1647      The proposed rule would establish a fee of $70,000 per F-1 
  1648  nonimmigrant
  1649  
  1650  [[Page 64577]]
  1651  
  1652  student applicable to SEVP-certified schools that recommend an F-1 
  1653  nonimmigrant student to engage in OPT for the first time. See proposed 
  1654  8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii) and 214.13(i)(1). This fee amount would apply to 
  1655  any type of OPT that the student participates in for the first time 
  1656  (irrespective of whether it is pre-completion OPT or post-completion 
  1657  OPT). Id. The initial $70,000 is a one-time fee that an SEVP-certified 
  1658  educational institution must pay for each F-1 nonimmigrant student 
  1659  prior to a DSO's initial recommendation of an F-1 nonimmigrant student 
  1660  to participate in any type of OPT under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii) for the 
  1661  first time. To be clear, this OPT fee would not be tied to a specific 
  1662  employer; rather the OPT fee would be applicable when a school decides 
  1663  to recommend an F-1 nonimmigrant student for any type of OPT.
  1664      The proposed rule would also establish a fee of $30,000 per F-1 
  1665  nonimmigrant student applicable to SEVP-certified schools that make any

Abstract:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is amending the regulations concerning the 9-11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee for certain H-1B and L-1 Visas (9-11 Biometric Fee). The regulatory changes correct DHS's interpretation of statutory language to require that covered employers submit the 9-11 Biometric Fee for all extension of status petitions, regardless of whether the related fraud prevention and detection fee applies, which includes extension of status petitions that do not involve a change of employer. The 9-11 Biometric Fee continues to apply unchanged to petitions seeking an initial grant of status. The changes also help DHS comply with its congressional mandate to implement a biometric entry-exit system.

   244  U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), U.S. Customs and 
   245  Border Protection (CBP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)

   255  coordination.\2\ The proposed H-1B fee is intended to provide a

   518  proposed rule by increasing fees broadly across all fee-paying 
   519  applicants and petitioners but determined that doing so would place 
   520  additional costs on individual applicants and petitioners, including 
   521  requestors whose applications and petitions may be less directly 
   522  connected to employment-based petitioning and who may have fewer 
   523  resources available to absorb additional fee increases. After 
   524  considering the resources of the different communities and populations 
   525  that submit immigration benefit requests to USCIS, DHS has decided to 
   526  propose that the costs be recovered by adding a fee to H-1B cap-subject 
   527  petitions. DHS considered other options but determined that shifting 
   528  these costs to petitioners for H-1B cap-subject petitions was 
   529  appropriate considering that they are requests that are generally 
   530  submitted by petitioners who have more ability to pay, as opposed to 
   531  shifting those costs to all other fee payers.\12\

   205  II. Executive Summary
   206  
   207  A. Purpose and Summary of the Regulatory Action
   208  
   209      The purpose of this proposed rule is to remove the availability of 
   210  the up to 60-day discretionary grace period from the regulations at 8 
   211  CFR 214.1(l)(2). The up to 60-day discretionary grace period 
   212  disconnects the alien's lawful status from the very basis of 
   213  eligibility under these employment-based nonimmigrant classifications. 
   214  By statute, an alien's lawful status in E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B, H-1B1, L-
   215  1, O-1, or TN nonimmigrant classification is directly connected to and 
   216  contingent upon the alien conducting certain employment activities or 
   217  otherwise providing services in the United States that is generally 
   218  tied to a petitioning employer. In order for an alien in any one of 
   219  these classifications to maintain his or her status, the alien 
   220  generally must maintain the employment or continue to perform the 
   221  activity that was the basis of the alien's eligibility for the 
   222  classification and associated admission or grant of status. However, 
   223  under current regulations, these aliens, and their dependents, are not 
   224  considered to have failed to maintain nonimmigrant status for a grace 
   225  period of up to 60 days following cessation of the employment or 
   226  activity that was the basis of their nonimmigrant status, unless that 
   227  grace period is shortened or eliminated as a matter of DHS discretion. 
   228  Typically, the decision whether or not to shorten or eliminate the 
   229  grace period is made by DHS when a petitioner submits a petition on 
   230  behalf of an alien, or the alien submits an application on behalf of 
   231  him or herself, which seeks to extend the stay or change or adjust the 
   232  status of the alien following the cessation of employment or activity 
   233  that was the basis of his or her initial classification or grant of 
   234  status.
   235      The proposed rule, by removing the up to 60-day discretionary grace 
   236  period, would better align the regulations with the statutory 
   237  provisions governing the relevant classifications by requiring an alien 
   238  to depart from the United States immediately upon his or her failure to 
   239  maintain the employment or activity that was the basis for the 
   240  nonimmigrant classification or status (unless otherwise authorized to 
   241  lawfully remain in the United States). It would also reduce the 
   242  administrative burden on USCIS associated with the grace period.
   243      DHS originally extended this grace period to aliens in the listed 
   244  classifications, and their dependents, to encourage aliens who ceased 
   245  employment prior to the end of the petition validity period to remain 
   246  in the United States to pursue other immigration options to maintain a 
   247  lawful immigration status and, depending on the classification sought, 
   248  continue or regain employment authorization; and to help U.S. employers 
   249  to more easily facilitate changes in employment for existing and newly 
   250  recruited nonimmigrant workers.\1\ However, the relevant rulemaking did 
   251  not sufficiently consider the negative impacts of the grace period 
   252  provision. Upon reconsideration, and consistent with the Secretary of 
   253  Homeland Security's (Secretary) broad authority to set the time and 
   254  conditions of admission of nonimmigrants and to require that they 
   255  depart the United States upon failure to maintain the employment or 
   256  activity that was the basis for the classification or status, DHS 
   257  believes that removing the up to 60-day discretionary grace period 
   258  through this proposed rule is necessary to better align the regulations 
   259  with the statutory basis for nonimmigrant status and to reduce 
   260  administrative burden associated with administering the grace period.
   261  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   262  
   263      \1\ See Retention of EB-1, EB-2, EB-3 Immigrant Workers and 
   264  Program Improvements Affecting High-Skilled Nonimmigrant Workers, 81 
   265  FR 82398 (Nov. 18, 2016) (``This grace period allows high-skilled 
   266  workers in these classifications, including those whose employment 
   267  ceases prior to the end of the petition validity period, to more 
   268  readily pursue new employment should they be eligible for other 
   269  employer-sponsored nonimmigrant classifications or employment in the 
   270  same classification with a new employer. The grace period also

93k tokens left (I started 240). Should research remaining Q7 9-11 fee, proclamation EO other docs, Q10, Q16 readmission ambiguity, final changes 5, Q6 later possible delay etc. I can do targeted.

Q5 conclusion possible transfer after completion, first academic year completed (Aug2025-May2027 >), f8iG within 5 months May14-Aug23 (101 days). Since not OPT. f5iiD EOS if seeking extension. f8iii change level via transfer procedures. f8iv new program beyond current period EOS. m1 requires EOS. Later delay authority through Sep14 2028 could suspend A-C (the crucial higher progression remains unaffected B) but search no notices as of today. Could DHS extend OPT I539 no bearing. Response yes if transfer procedures initiated at/after completion; if while currently graduate, f8iC requires narrow SEVP exception. Most defensible yes after completion. Uncertainty timing of release if school releases earlier: f8iG earlier of transfer out or completion. Should mention release at current session completion or expected transfer earlier f8ii. If release before May14, deadline earlier. And f8iC ambiguity if process initiated pre completion. Rule f8iii higher change can use transfer, so yes.

Q6 Ahmed completes Dec11 after effective, same MBA. f5iiC cannot maintain/admitted/provided F1 at same/lower; blocks both transfer and reentry. f5iiB only higher. f8i also transfer eligibility but f5iiC supersedes. (b) August2027 start within 5 months Dec11 +5 = May11 2027, so August outside even apart from same level. f8iG earlier transfer out/completion. (c) program end Dec11 +60 = Feb9 2027 (Dec remaining20 days to Dec31? Dec11 +60 Feb9: 20 days Dec31 +31 Jan=51 +9=60). cap no issue. (d) DHS can delay/suspend f5iiA-C until Sep14 2028 f5iiE, by FR notice and SEVP, could change before Aug2027; later final amendment or litigation general? Rule severability. Search no notice. Proposed OPT not change same-level. Response could change via suspension before Aug. Also 5 month rule not A-C? f8iG wouldn't be suspended. So even if C suspended, transfer timing would independently block transfer Aug but reentry routecould work if C suspended. Ask "answer a change" yes potentially but transfer still timing bar. Good.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

    30  SUMMARY: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is amending the 
    31  regulations concerning the 9-11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee 
    32  for certain H-1B and L-1 Visas (9-11 Biometric Fee). The regulatory 
    33  changes correct DHS's interpretation of statutory language to require 
    34  that covered employers submit the 9-11 Biometric Fee for all extension 
    35  of status petitions, regardless of whether the related fraud prevention 
    36  and detection fee applies, which includes extension of status petitions 
    37  that do not involve a change of employer. The 9-11 Biometric Fee 
    38  continues to apply unchanged to petitions seeking an initial grant of 
    39  status. The changes also help DHS comply with its congressional mandate 
    40  to implement a biometric entry-exit system.
    41  
    42  DATES: This rule is effective on September 9, 2026.

    49  
    50  I. Background
    51  
    52  A. Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

    54      On June 6, 2024, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) 
    55  published a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) in the Federal 
    56  Register (89 FR 48339) proposing to amend DHS regulations regarding the 
    57  9-11 Biometric Fee for certain H-1B and L-1 petitions. DHS received a 
    58  total of 146 comments on the NPRM. Comments included support, 
    59  suggestions for changes, and concerns. After review of the comments, 
    60  through this final rule, DHS is adopting the proposed changes to its 
    61  regulations to align with Congress's intent for the 9-11 Biometric Fee.
    62  
    63  B. Statutory Authorization and History
    64  
    65  1. Initial Supplemental H-1B and L-1 Fee
    66      H-1B and L-1 visa classifications are temporary nonimmigrant worker 
    67  visa classifications. H-1B and L-1 classifications \1\ are authorized

    69  Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), as amended (8 U.S.C. 
    70  1101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b), (L)). H-1B status is a nonimmigrant 
    71  classification for aliens to perform services in a specialty 
    72  occupation. L-1 status allows companies to seek a temporary 
    73  intracompany transfer of certain alien

   100  than 50 percent of the employees in the United States in H-1B or L-1 
   101  nonimmigrant status (covered employers). Sec. 402, Public Law 111-230. 
   102  For these covered employers, the statute stated ``the filing fee and 
   103  fraud prevention and detection fee [. . .] shall be increased by $2,000

   105  Law 111-230.

   107  employers to pay the 2010 Supplemental Fee at the time that a fraud 
   108  detection and prevention fee (Fraud Fee) is collected. Sec. 402, Public

   115  Fraud Fee collections to combat fraud in immigration processes. See INA 
   116  214(c)(12)(A) (8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(12)(A), see also INA 286(v)(2) (8 
   117  U.S.C. 1356(v)(2)). With limited exceptions, the statute requires 
   118  employers to pay the Fraud Fee when petitioning for an initial grant of 
   119  H-1B or L-1 nonimmigrant status or for change of employer petitions for 
   120  beneficiaries already in H-1B or L-1 status. See INA 214(c)(12)(A) (8 
   121  U.S.C. 1184(c)(12)(A)).
   122      DHS interpreted the statutory language of Public Law 111-230 to 
   123  mean that the 2010 Supplemental Fee only applied to the filing fee and 
   124  only to petitions where the Fraud Fee also applied, namely petitions 
   125  for an initial grant of status or requesting a change of employer but 
   126  not to extension petitions filed by the same employer on behalf of the

   128  2010 Supplemental Fee to petitions subject to the Fraud Fee seeking

   130  for beneficiaries already in H-1B or L-1 status. See Immigration 
   131  Benefits Business Transformation, Increment I, 76 FR 53764, 53768,

   160  fees for H-1B and L-1 visas. Accordingly, the subject heading of

   162  1B and L-1 visas.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

    30                  By the authority vested in me as President by the

    33  
    34                  Section 1. Purpose. The H-1B nonimmigrant visa program 
    35                  was created to identify uniquely skilled and highly 
    36                  specialized foreign temporary workers to strategically 
    37                  supplement the United States economy. Instead, the 
    38                  program has been widely abused by certain employers, 
    39                  third-party placement groups, and outsourcing firms to 
    40                  undercut and displace the supply of skilled United 
    41                  States labor. The large-scale, systematic abuse of the 
    42                  H-1B program to obtain non-qualifying foreign labor has 
    43                  undermined the additive purpose of the program and 
    44                  harmed the wages, working conditions, and job 
    45                  opportunities of skilled American workers.
    46  
    47                  The abuse of cheaper H-1B labor places downward 
    48                  pressure on domestic pay. H-1B visa holders earn far 
    49                  less than comparable United States-born workers, 
    50                  despite the statutory mandate that H-1B workers be paid 
    51                  equally to their domestic peers, with the estimated 
    52                  wage gap starting at $9,000 and climbing as high as 
    53                  $20,000 in H-1B reliant industries. One company even 
    54                  warned its shareholders that restrictions on cheap H-1B 
    55                  labor could force the company to use ``local'' workers, 
    56                  which ``may only be available at higher wages.''
    57  
    58                  Many employers have laid off large numbers of highly 
    59                  skilled American workers, only to promptly hire large 
    60                  numbers of H-1B workers who are often lower-skilled and 
    61                  lower-paid. For instance, technology sector employers 
    62                  have collectively requested H-1B visas for hundreds of 
    63                  thousands of workers, yet have also laid off somewhere 
    64                  between 800,000 to 1.3 million American employees from 
    65                  2022 through 2026. Employers have even forced laid off 
    66                  American workers to train their foreign replacements.
    67  
    68                  Many jobs held by H-1B workers eventually leave the 
    69                  United States entirely. Employers with outsourcing 
    70                  business models use teams of H-1B visa holders to 
    71                  replace United States workers at third-party client 
    72                  businesses and liaise with other individuals working 
    73                  off-site from their country of origin. As soon as 
    74                  practicable, much of their own work is transferred 
    75                  offshore. In Fiscal Year 2026, the top six users of the 
    76                  H-1B program operating with this outsourcing business 
    77                  model accounted for over 25,000 H-1B cap registrations. 
    78                  One foreign country's foreign minister even publicly 
    79                  admitted that H-1B ``has become the outsourcing visa.''
    80  
    81                  The systematic and organized abuse of the H-1B program 
    82                  is also a national security threat. Domestic law 
    83                  enforcement agencies have investigated H-1B-reliant 
    84                  outsourcing firms for engaging in visa fraud, 
    85                  conspiracy to launder money, and other illicit 
    86                  activities to encourage foreign workers to come to the 
    87                  United States. Abuses of the H-1B program also present 
    88                  a national security threat by discouraging Americans 
    89                  from pursuing careers in science and technology, 
    90                  risking vital United States leadership in these fields.

    93                  have flagged employers' large-scale, systematic abuse 
    94                  of the H-1B program to obtain lower-paid, lower-skilled 
    95                  labor from abroad. These ongoing Government probes 
    96                  continue to identify widespread fraud and noncompliance 
    97                  among H-1B

Q1.answer:
(a) The final rule is **“Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media,” FR document 2026-14439, 91 FR 44976–45131**.

(b) It was **published July 17, 2026**, and its stated effective date was **September 15, 2026**. It is in effect on the research date.

(c) **DHS Docket No. ICEB-2025-0001; RIN 1653-AA95**.

(d) It finalized the NPRM bearing the same title, **FR document 2025-16554, 90 FR 42070–42115**, published **August 28, 2025**. The ordinary comment deadline was September 29, 2025, and the information-collection deadline was October 27, 2025.

(e) No later Federal Register document through November 14, 2026 was found changing that effective date. The final rule, however, says that it is a major rule subject to congressional review and that, **at the conclusion of that review, if the effective date has changed, DHS will publish a document establishing the actual effective date or terminating the rule**. Thus September 15, 2026 remains the operative date, but the rule itself preserves the possibility of a later Federal Register change or termination.

Q2.answer:
(a) Priya may remain without filing through **July 14, 2027**. The transition provision uses the later of the EAD expiration or the I-20 program end date, subject to the four-year cap, and adds 60 days for an F student. She has no EAD, so: **May 15, 2027 + 60 days = July 14, 2027**. This does not extend ordinary on-campus employment beyond the program end; the provision separately limits employment/training continuation to the program end or EAD expiration.

(b) The absolute transition maxima are:
- **F nonimmigrants: November 14, 2030**, calculated as **September 15, 2026 + 4 years = September 15, 2030; + 60 days = November 14, 2030**.
- **J nonimmigrants: October 15, 2030**, calculated as **September 15, 2026 + 4 years = September 15, 2030; + 30 days = October 15, 2030**.
These dates are expressly stated in the rule and apply only if the person otherwise remains in valid status.

(c) **Yes, timing permits the transfer.** She completed a bachelor’s and will begin a higher educational level, so the upward-progression rule is satisfied. The transfer rule requires classes to begin within five months after the earlier of transfer-out or the program-completion date. Using her May 15 completion date: **May 15, 2027 + 5 calendar months = October 15, 2027**. Her **August 24, 2027** start is within that window. If the actual transfer-out/release date were earlier than completion, that earlier date would start the five-month period. She also completed more than her first academic year and is not transferring mid-course from one graduate program to another.

(d) **Yes. Because the new program extends beyond her transition-authorized stay, she must obtain an extension of stay, ordinarily on Form I-539, from USCIS.** A SEVIS transfer and new I-20 alone do not extend her stay. USCIS should receive the application by **July 14, 2027**, the end of her transition period. She submits the new properly endorsed I-20, evidence of sufficient funds, the fee and any required biometrics. Her transfer/change to a higher level is accomplished through the transfer procedures, but the separate EOS requirement remains. Filing in the departure period can be timely but would not preserve uninterrupted employment.

(e) Under the transition OPT exemption, Priya need file **only Form I-765 for the requested post-completion OPT; she need not file Form I-539**. Her March 1, 2027 filing is on or before March 18, 2027 and before expiration of her transition stay, including its 60-day departure period. The requested June 14 start is exactly 30 days after the May 15 program end.

If approved as requested, she may remain through **August 12, 2028**: **June 13, 2028 EAD/OPT expiration + 60 days = August 12, 2028**. Approval is necessary before she can work in OPT.

Q3.answer:
(a) The earliest permissible entry was **December 13, 2026**: **January 12, 2027 program start − 30 days = December 13, 2026**. His December 20 entry was within the arrival window.

(b) His I-94 admit-until date should be **January 17, 2028**. The program is shorter than four years, so: **December 18, 2027 I-20 program end + 30 days = January 17, 2028**.

(c) **Yes.** An unexpected change in faculty advisor is expressly an “unexpected research problem,” and therefore a compelling academic reason supporting an extension under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(i)**. One expressly unacceptable reason is **academic probation or suspension**; another is the student’s repeated inability or unwillingness to complete the course of study.

(d) The DSO must enter the extension **before the existing I-20 program end date, December 18, 2027**. The October 2027 update is timely. A DSO entry after that date does not merely produce an ordinary extension: the student must seek **reinstatement of F-1 status**, with the required form, fee and any biometrics; the DSO’s action by itself never extends USCIS-authorized stay.

(e) For uninterrupted RA employment, USCIS must receive the EOS **on or before December 18, 2027**, the program/employment end date. A filing received later but **on or before January 17, 2028**, the I-94 expiration including the 30-day period, remains timely for the EOS. Its consequence is loss of uninterrupted work authorization: he may continue a full course of study while the timely application is pending but may not continue or begin employment until approval. A receipt after January 17 is not timely under the F-1 provision.

(f) A qualifying timely filing keeps the RA authorization going while the EOS is pending, but the automatic employment extension is capped at **240 days from the January 17, 2028 I-94 admission end date**, or an earlier USCIS decision or other applicable limit. **January 17, 2028 + 240 days = approximately September 13, 2028** (2028 is a leap year). After 240 days he must stop working if the application is still pending, although authorized stay and full-time study may continue until decision.

(g) If approved for the new I-20 end date, his authorized stay ends **June 18, 2028**: **May 19, 2028 + 30 days = June 18, 2028**. If USCIS denies after January 17, 2028 has passed, he and any dependents must **depart immediately**; no further departure grace period is supplied.

Q4.answer:
(a) **He can make the trip without automatically abandoning the pending I-539, provided he returns before his previously authorized period expires and seeks admission only for the balance of that period.** His prior I-94 period runs through January 17, 2028, so his January 5 return is before expiration.

**Presentation at re-entry matters.** If he seeks admission for the balance of the previous period, USCIS will not consider the timely EOS abandoned. If he instead seeks admission using the I-20 with the later May 19, 2028 end date to obtain a new period beyond the previous admission, the pending EOS **may be deemed abandoned**. Corresponding employment-authorization applications are not considered abandoned on that basis.

He should carry his **Form I-797C receipt for the pending I-539** and evidence of the proposed length of stay, particularly the **current Form I-20** (the rule also lists a DS-2019 or employer letter for other classifications). Admission and the period granted remain CBP decisions.

(b) For a **change** from F-1 to another nonimmigrant status, departure while the change-of-status application is pending causes USCIS to consider that application **abandoned**. This differs from the special preservation rule for a timely F/J/I extension-of-stay application described in (a).

Q5.answer:
**Conclusion: Mei can transfer her SEVIS record from School A to School B for the PhD if the transfer is processed after she has completed the master’s, without needing the narrow mid-program graduate-transfer exception. Her timing and upward educational progression qualify. A transfer attempted while she is still “currently in” the master’s program would require an SEVP extenuating-circumstances exception.**

The final provisions apply as follows:

- **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A):** a graduate student may not transfer at any point **during** the program unless SEVP authorizes an extenuating-circumstances exception. Mei should therefore not use an ordinary mid-master’s transfer. The exception is narrow and not a general vehicle for academic advancement.
- **(f)(5)(ii)(B):** a student who completes a program at one level and begins another at a **higher** level maintains F-1 status if otherwise compliant. Master’s to PhD fits this express progression.
- **(f)(5)(ii)(C):** completion after September 15, 2026 bars a new F-1 program at the **same or a lower**, not higher, level. Her May 14, 2027 master’s completion triggers the provision but the PhD does not violate it.
- **(f)(5)(ii)(D):** if an extension is needed for the change in educational objective, she must apply for it with the required form, fee, evidence and any biometrics. It does not replace the transfer procedure.
- **(f)(8)(i)(A)–(F):** she must be maintaining status; completion of a degree satisfies (B)(2); the first-academic-year requirement is met because she began at School A in August 2025; no probation or disqualifying pattern is assumed. The “not currently in a graduate level program” condition in (C) is why processing after completion is the clean reading. If she is still currently enrolled when eligibility is assessed, an SEVP exception is required.
- **(f)(8)(i)(G):** School B classes must begin within five months after the earlier of transfer-out or program completion. From **May 14, 2027 + 5 months = October 14, 2027**, so **August 23, 2027** is timely. An earlier release/transfer-out date would move the deadline earlier.
- **(f)(8)(ii):** School A marks transfer-out and sets a release date, controls the record until the current term ends or that date arrives, after which School B controls and issues the new I-20.
- **(f)(8)(iii):** a change in education level may use those transfer procedures.
- **(f)(8)(iv)** and **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1):** because the PhD will extend beyond her D/S-transition stay, she must also obtain a USCIS EOS for that added period; the transfer itself does not authorize the extra stay.

DHS may delay or suspend **(f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C)** until September 14, 2028 by Federal Register notice and SEVP announcement. That could relax the same/lower-level and mid-program restrictions, but would not eliminate the separate five-month transfer-timing rule or EOS requirement. No such notice or other later document changing this conclusion was located through November 14, 2026.

Admission to and approval of the new USCIS EOS remain discretionary.
